extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, federal judges, and patent law scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Legal framework and criteria used to determine whether prosecution history estoppel bars reliance on the doctrine of equivalents after a claim-narrowing amendment (as articulated by the Federal Circuit on remand from the Supreme Court in Festo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Whether the amendment narrowed the literal scope of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The first question in a prosecution history estoppel inquiry is whether an amendment filed in the PTO has narrowed the literal scope of a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the amendment was not narrowing, prosecution history estoppel does not apply. (Cites Pioneer Magnetics v. Micro Linear.) This is a threshold factual/legal determination to be resolved before proceeding to reasons for the amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 — Whether the amendment was made for a substantial reason relating to patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: If the amendment was narrowing, the second question is whether the reason for that amendment was a substantial one relating to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the prosecution history record reveals no reason for the narrowing amendment, the Warner-Jenkinson presumption treats the amendment as made for a substantial reason relating to patentability. A patentee seeking to rebut that Warner-Jenkinson presumption must do so based on the prosecution history record (to preserve the public notice function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Festo presumption of surrender (scope surrendered by a patentability-related narrowing amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a narrowing amendment is found to have been made for a reason relating to patentability, Festo imposes the presumption that the patentee surrendered all territory between the original claim limitation and the amended claim limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a rebuttable presumption; the patentee bears the burden to show that the particular alleged equivalent was not surrendered. If the patentee fails to rebut, prosecution history estoppel bars reliance on the doctrine of equivalents for that claim limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's burden to rebut the Festo presumption (general statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must show that 'at the time of the amendment one skilled in the art could not reasonably be expected to have drafted a claim that would have literally encompassed the alleged equivalent.' (Festo VIII, 535 U.S. at 741.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court enumerated three ways to overcome the presumption; the patentee must prove at least one of them. The court treats the ultimate rebuttal determination as a question of law for the court to decide, though underlying factual issues may exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal criterion 1 — Unforeseeability (objective inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee may rebut the presumption by demonstrating that the alleged equivalent would have been unforeseeable to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an objective inquiry about the state of the art and understanding of a hypothetical person of ordinary skill at the time the narrowing amendment was made (not at the time of original application). Later-developed technology or technology not known in the relevant art is typically unforeseeable; equivalents known in the prior art are generally foreseeable. Because this depends on underlying facts (e.g., state of the art), a district court may hear expert testimony and consider extrinsic evidence on foreseeability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal criterion 2 — Tangential relation of the amendment's rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee may rebut the presumption by demonstrating that 'the rationale underlying the amendment bore no more than a tangential relation to the equivalent in question.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion asks whether the reason for narrowing was peripheral or not directly relevant to the alleged equivalent. An amendment made to avoid prior art that contains the equivalent is not tangential. The inquiry focuses on the objectively apparent reason for the amendment as discernible from the prosecution history record; determination of tangentialness is for the court and generally limited to the prosecution history (with testimony from those skilled in the art permitted when necessary to interpret the record).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal criterion 3 — 'Some other reason' the patentee could not reasonably be expected to have described the equivalent
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee may rebut the presumption by showing 'some other reason' suggesting that the patentee could not reasonably be expected to have described the insubstantial substitute in question (e.g., shortcomings of language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a narrow, catch-all category intended for exceptional circumstances (for example, linguistic limitations). When possible, determinations under this criterion should be limited to the prosecution history record. A patentee may not rely on this criterion when the alleged equivalent is in the prior art (because then there is no other reason the patentee could not have described it). The court left unresolved what, if any, evidence outside the prosecution history may be considered under this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing rule for foreseeability
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant time for assessing foreseeability is when the narrowing amendment was made, not the time of the original application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies when the hypothetical skilled artisan's knowledge is to be measured — the instant the patentee presumptively surrendered subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of evidence for rebutting the Warner-Jenkinson presumption (reason for amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee's rebuttal of the Warner-Jenkinson presumption as to why an amendment was made is restricted to the prosecution history record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation is to preserve the public notice function of the patent and its prosecution history; allowing evidence outside the public record to establish reason would undermine that notice function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of judge and jury in rebuttal determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations concerning whether the presumption of surrender has arisen and whether it has been rebutted are questions of law for the court, not for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although factual issues underlie some rebuttal inquiries (e.g., unforeseeability), resolution of these underlying facts may be made by the court; prosecution history estoppel is equitable and functions as a legal limitation on remedies, placing the ultimate decision within the court's province.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of failure or success in rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee fails to rebut the Festo presumption of surrender, prosecution history estoppel bars the patentee from relying on the doctrine of equivalents for the accused element; if the patentee successfully rebuts, estoppel does not apply and equivalence is considered on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the practical stakes for proving one of the rebuttal criteria — failure forecloses DOE for that limitation; success returns the case to ordinary equivalence analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement of related holdings (voluntary amendments and §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrowing amendment made to comply with any provision of the Patent Act (including §112) may give rise to estoppel; a 'voluntary' amendment (not required by examiner and not made in response to a stated rejection) may give rise to prosecution history estoppel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prior en banc holdings were reinstated: amendments for §112 or other statutory requirements may invoke estoppel, and voluntary amendments can give rise to estoppel. Also, when the prosecution history reveals no stated reason, Warner-Jenkinson presumes a patentability-related reason and Festo then presumes surrender of the intervening territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of Warner-Jenkinson and Festo presumptions (procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Warner-Jenkinson presumption (that an unexplained narrowing amendment was for a substantial reason related to patentability) and the Festo presumption (that such an amendment surrenders all territory between original and amended limitations) operate together in sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: (1) Determine if amendment narrowed claim; (2) if so, determine whether amendment was for patentability (Warner-Jenkinson presumes yes if reason not in record); (3) if patentability-related, apply Festo presumption of surrender; (4) allow patentee to attempt rebuttal via the three Festo criteria; (5) if unsuccessful, estoppel bars DOE; if successful, proceed to equivalence merits.
